content.text: Gravitation describes the mutual attraction between material bodies. Objects thrown upward return toward Earth, rain falls toward Earth, and planetary motions are governed by gravitational attraction. Galileo recognised that bodies fall with the same acceleration irrespective of their masses, neglecting relevant effects such as air resistance.

Ptolemy's geocentric model placed Earth at the centre and used complicated circular motions to explain planetary observations. Aryabhata discussed a heliocentric model in the fifth century A.D. Copernicus later proposed planets revolving around the Sun. Tycho Brahe recorded planetary observations, which Johannes Kepler analysed to formulate three laws of planetary motion.

Every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse can be drawn by keeping a string taut between two fixed foci. For any point on an ellipse, the sum of distances to the two foci is constant. The closest point to the Sun is perihelion; the farthest is aphelion. The semi-major axis is half the major axis. A circle is a special case of an ellipse.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Kepler's first law: law of orbits

content.text: The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. A planet moves faster when nearer the Sun and slower when farther away. For a central force, angular momentum is conserved, leading to constant areal velocity.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Kepler's second law: law of areas

content.text: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.
equations: T²/a³ = constant for planets orbiting the same central body

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Kepler's third law: law of periods

content.text: The chapter compares the semi-major axes and orbital periods of Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Their approximate T²/a³ values are nearly constant, confirming Kepler's third law. The table uses a in units of 10¹⁰ m and T in years; the listed quotient is in units of 10⁻³⁴ y² m⁻³.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Planetary data and Kepler's third law

content.text: For a central force directed along the radius vector, the torque about the centre is zero. Angular momentum remains constant, and the areal velocity is constant. This explains Kepler's law of areas and applies to any central force, not only inverse-square gravity.

Every body in the universe attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. The force is attractive and acts along the line joining the bodies.

For point masses, the gravitational force is directed along the line joining them and has magnitude Gm₁m₂/r². The vector expression encodes the attractive direction; forces on the two bodies are equal and opposite, consistent with Newton's third law.

When several masses act on a particle, the net gravitational force is the vector sum of the individual forces exerted by each mass. The force due to each mass can be calculated independently and then added vectorially.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Principle of superposition of gravitational forces

content.text: For a uniform hollow spherical shell, the force on an external point mass is the same as if the entire shell's mass were concentrated at its centre. The net gravitational force at a point inside a complete uniform spherical shell is zero. A shell does not shield outside gravitational influences.

The universal gravitational constant G appears in Newton's law of gravitation. Its value given in the chapter is approximately 6.672 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Cavendish's experiment measures G through the small gravitational attraction between masses.

Cavendish used a torsion balance: two small lead spheres attached to a suspended bar were attracted by nearby large lead spheres. The forces produce a torque and twist the fine suspension wire. The deflection enables the gravitational attraction and hence G to be determined.

For a body of mass m at Earth's surface, gravitational force is GM_E m/R_E². Equating this to mg gives the surface acceleration due to gravity. The mass of Earth can be related to g, G and Earth's radius.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface

content.text: At altitude h above Earth's surface, distance from Earth's centre is R_E + h. The gravitational acceleration decreases with altitude according to the inverse-square law.

When altitude h is much smaller than Earth's radius, the expression for gravitational acceleration can be approximated by expanding in h/R_E. This shows that g decreases approximately linearly with small altitude.

Assuming Earth has uniform density, only the mass within radius R_E − d contributes to gravity at depth d. The gravitational acceleration decreases linearly with depth and becomes zero at Earth's centre.

The value of g decreases with increasing altitude because the distance from Earth's centre increases. Under the uniform-density assumption, g also decreases with depth and is zero at the centre. These relations depend on the stated approximations.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Variation of g with altitude and depth

content.text: Gravitational force is conservative, so gravitational potential energy can be defined. For two point masses separated by distance r, choosing potential energy zero at infinity gives a negative potential energy.

The change in gravitational potential energy between radii r₁ and r₂ equals the difference of potential energies at those positions. Only the difference is physically meaningful; the zero level can be chosen by convention.

The familiar expression mgh is an approximation to the change in gravitational potential energy when the height difference is small compared with Earth's radius, so g can be treated as nearly constant.

Gravitational potential at a point is potential energy per unit mass. For a point mass M, taking the potential to be zero at infinity, the potential is negative and depends inversely on distance from the mass.

Escape speed is the minimum initial speed required for an object projected from a celestial body's surface to reach infinity with zero final speed, neglecting other bodies and atmospheric resistance. It is independent of the mass of the escaping object.

Conservation of mechanical energy relates the initial kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy to the energy at infinity. Escape is possible when the initial total energy is non-negative; the minimum escape speed corresponds to zero total energy.
For launch from distance r from Earth's centre, the escape speed follows from setting the initial kinetic energy equal to the magnitude of gravitational potential energy at that radius.

Earth satellites revolve around Earth under gravity, in a manner analogous to planets revolving around the Sun. A satellite in a circular orbit is continuously accelerated toward Earth; gravity provides the required centripetal force.
For a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r around Earth, equating gravitational force to centripetal force gives the orbital speed. The result does not depend on the satellite's mass.

For circular satellite motion, orbital period follows from circumference divided by orbital speed. The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius for satellites orbiting the same central body.

An astronaut in an orbiting satellite experiences apparent weightlessness because both the astronaut and the satellite are in free fall under Earth's gravity. It is not because gravity is absent or necessarily very small.

The total mechanical energy of a satellite is the sum of its kinetic and gravitational potential energies. For a circular orbit, kinetic energy is positive, potential energy is negative, and total energy is negative.
The energy needed to take a satellite from a circular orbit to infinity with zero final speed is the magnitude of its negative total orbital energy, if the change is made without other energy losses.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Energy required to remove a satellite from orbit

content.text: A satellite's orbital period depends on its orbital radius. A satellite with a period matching Earth's rotation can remain over approximately the same point on Earth's equator when it moves in the appropriate direction in a circular equatorial orbit.
Kepler's laws apply to satellites orbiting Earth as well as planets orbiting the Sun. For satellites around the same central body, the ratio T²/r³ is constant for circular orbits.

Using conservation of angular momentum for a planet at perihelion and aphelion, the position and velocity vectors are perpendicular at these points. The angular momentum relation gives r_P v_P = r_A v_A; since r_A > r_P, the speed at perihelion is greater.
equations: m r_P v_P = m r_A v_A

content.text: Using Kepler's third law, the orbital period of Mars can be estimated from its mean Sun-distance relative to Earth's. With the distance ratio about 1.52 and Earth's period 365 days, the chapter obtains approximately 684 days.

metadata.topic: Worked example: estimating Mars's orbital period

content.text: Earth's mass can be estimated from the surface value of g, Earth's radius and the gravitational constant using g = GM_E/R_E². The chapter also discusses using the Moon's orbital period and distance to infer the Earth's mass.

The Moon's centripetal acceleration is determined from its orbital radius and period. It is much smaller than the acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface, consistent with the decrease of gravitational acceleration with distance.

The gravitational force between two point masses is calculated using the product of their masses, the square of the separation and G. For extended spherical bodies, when the point lies outside a spherically symmetric body, its mass can be treated as concentrated at the centre.

metadata.topic: Worked example: gravitational force between bodies

content.text: Energy conservation can be used to find the minimum speed needed for a projectile to escape Earth's gravitational influence. The minimum case has zero total energy at infinity.

content.text: Newton's law states that the gravitational force between masses m₁ and m₂ separated by distance r has magnitude Gm₁m₂/r². The force is attractive, and multiple contributions are combined using superposition.
At Earth's surface, g = GM_E/R_E². Gravity decreases with altitude according to the inverse-square relation and, for a uniform-density Earth, decreases linearly with depth.
Gravitational potential energy for two masses is conventionally −Gm₁m₂/r when zero is chosen at infinity. Escape speed from Earth's surface is √(2gR_E).

For a circular orbit, gravitational attraction supplies centripetal force. Orbital speed is √(GM_E/r), and the orbital period obeys T² = 4π²r³/(GM_E). The total energy of a circular orbit is negative.

For motion under gravitational influence of another object, angular momentum and total mechanical energy are conserved, while the linear momentum of the orbiting object alone is not necessarily conserved.
Angular momentum conservation leads to Kepler's second law. This result is not unique to inverse-square gravitation; it holds for any central force.

metadata.topic: Points to ponder: central forces and Kepler's second law

content.text: In Kepler's third law, T² = K R³, the constant K is the same for bodies orbiting the same central body. The relationship also applies to satellites orbiting Earth.

metadata.topic: Points to ponder: same central body

content.text: Astronauts experience apparent weightlessness in orbit because they and their spacecraft are in free fall together, not because gravitational force has disappeared.
The gravitational potential energy expression may include an arbitrary additive constant. Choosing zero at infinity gives U = −Gm₁m₂/r. Changing this constant does not change gravitational force.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to ponder: arbitrary zero of potential energy

content.text: With potential energy zero at infinity, gravitational potential energy is negative. A satellite in a bound orbit has negative total mechanical energy.

metadata.topic: Points to ponder: total energy of a satellite

content.text: The expression mgh is an approximation for gravitational potential-energy change near Earth's surface where g is nearly constant.

The force between finite rigid bodies is not always directed along the line joining their centres of mass. For a spherically symmetric body and an external point, the force acts as if the body's mass were concentrated at its centre.

content.text: The gravitational force inside a complete uniform spherical shell is zero due to the shell itself, but gravitational shielding of external bodies is not possible.
